tip: After ताकि (taaki = so that), the verb takes its wish form – उठ सकूँ (uth sakoon), not the plain future उठूँगा (uthoonga).
To lead with the reason, use चूँकि (choonki = since), answered by इसलिए (isliye = so): चूँकि बारिश हो रही थी, इसलिए... क्योंकि (kyonki = because) usually follows the main clause instead.
हालाँकि (haalaanki = although) demands an answer in clause two: फिर भी (phir bhi = even so). Dropping the फिर भी sounds unfinished to Hindi ears.
In न सिर्फ़...बल्कि (na sirf...balki = not only...but rather), the 'also' splits off – भी (bhi) lands after the new item: पहला नंबर भी (pahla number bhi).
तो (to) after a whole clause means 'so': बीमार थी तो (beemaar thi to = she was sick, so...). No separate word for 'so' is needed.
तो (to) right after a word concedes it: मौसम तो ख़राब था (mausam to kharaab tha) = 'the weather WAS bad, sure' – and a पर (par = but) is coming.
वरना (varna = otherwise) flips to would-have mode: हो जाता (ho jaata) = would have happened. The bare -ता form carries the whole 'would have'.
You ask FROM someone in Hindi – शिक्षक से सवाल पूछा (shikshak se sawaal poochha): से (se = from) marks the person asked, not को (ko).
इसीलिए (isiliye) packs ही (hi = exactly) inside इसलिए (isliye = that's why): 'that's precisely why'. उसी को (usi ko) does the same – to her and no one else.
